source_note: Maria-style scenario · keyed line anchors on M.G. §10.1 verbatim opener. Distractors drawn from §10.4 P.B. + §11 GC-19/17/20.
stem: You're about to dial Maria, who owns a two-store retail business. Companies House shows she opened the second store in January. Which opener works as an M1 diagnostic?

choices.text: Hi Maria — do you have a moment to talk about your corporate spending?
choices.feedback: Too generic: no signal and no diagnostic question. When a bottom-quartile rep opened Maria's call this way, she hung up at 0:08.

choices.text: I noticed you opened a second location 6 months ago — who's approving expense reports across both stores now?
choices.feedback: Correct. It names a specific signal (the second location) and asks who controls what. M.G. opened this way and booked a demo 14 minutes into the call.

choices.text: Our card is cheaper than your bank's — worth 10 minutes?
choices.feedback: Arguing on fees is a pitch, not a diagnostic. A recorded call that opened this way ended at 0:24.

choices.text: We help SMB owners get real-time visibility into their team spend — can I tell you more?
choices.feedback: This goes straight into a pitch. On a recorded call with this opener, the buyer hung up at 0:22 because nobody asked a diagnostic question.

source_note: Worked-example completion on Tom · §12.2 Series-B founder · drives variability vs Maria. Keyed answer pairs signal with who-controls-what in ≤ 15 words.
stem: Tom just closed a Series B (LinkedIn announcement last month, 22 FTE, 6 engineering jobs posted). Which diagnostic pairs the signal with a who-controls-what question in 15 words or fewer?

choices.text: Congratulations on the Series B — that must be a huge milestone for the team. Would love to hear how it's going.
choices.feedback: Too long, and it asks nothing about who controls what. A compliment is not a diagnostic.

choices.text: Saw your Series B — who's owning per-employee card issuance now that engineering is scaling?
choices.feedback: Correct. 14 words, a specific signal (the Series B) and a who-controls-what question (per-employee card issuance). L.D. opened Tom's call the same way.

choices.text: We help fast-growing SaaS teams with corporate cards — sound like something you'd want to evaluate?
choices.feedback: A pitch with no signal. It fails the same way as the 'We help SMB owners' opener in question 1.
A yes/no question with no signal behind it. Even if Tom says yes, you have nothing to acknowledge in M2.

source_note: Threshold-concept item · anchored on M.G. §10.1 verbatim ('Ask one good question and then shut up for 5 seconds'). Distractors are §10.4 P.B. anti-patterns.
stem: You ask your diagnostic question. The buyer says nothing for 6 seconds: no breath you can hear, no reply. What do you do?

choices.text: Rephrase the question more clearly so they understand it.
choices.feedback: You just took the silence away. As M.G. puts it: 'Five seconds feels like an hour but it's where the deal happens.'

choices.text: Fill the gap with a quick benefit statement to keep momentum.
choices.feedback: This is the bottom-quartile reflex, the one P.B. shows. Pitching into the silence kills the diagnostic.

choices.text: Wait. Let the buyer fill the silence.
choices.feedback: Correct. Sit through the 5-second silence. The buyer is thinking, and what they say next is the real pain.

choices.text: Ask if they're still on the line.
choices.feedback: It breaks the silence and shows you're uncomfortable. The buyer hears a sales rep, not a peer.
